title: Effects of a change to more formative assessment among tertiary mathematics students
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether moving from largely summative assessment toward more formative assessment improves learning outcomes in a first-year university mathematics unit. The motivation is that many tertiary mathematics students struggle with the transition to university-level work, and large classes limit the amount of direct instructor support available. The authors ask whether giving students unlimited practice with computer-assisted feedback, plus a new written assignment focused on clear mathematical reasoning, leads to better understanding as reflected in final examination performance.

The intervention was introduced when a large Australian university changed from semesters to trimesters. Two adjacent cohorts in the same core Mathematics 1A unit were compared: Cohort 1 experienced the previous assessment structure, while Cohort 2 received online practice opportunities with feedback for class tests, tests completed under exam conditions in computer labs, and an added assignment on writing solutions and evidence. Both cohorts had the same syllabus, teaching hours, and materials, and final exam tasks were closely matched across years. Student solutions were scored using a SOLO-taxonomy-based rubric to compare levels of understanding.

Results favored the cohort exposed to the more formative assessment approach on nearly all tasks and on the composite score, with a moderate-to-high overall effect size. The score distributions also shifted away from very low scores, suggesting that the added practice and feedback helped more students get started and progress on problems. The authors conclude that the formative elements appeared to promote learning with understanding, though they note that the study only measured written examination outcomes and did not capture student attitudes, experiences, or longer-term effects.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental cohort comparison, not a randomized trial. It uses adjacent-year cohorts with comparable syllabus/materials and objective exam scoring, but there is no random assignment and limited control for confounding.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed impact is modest-to-moderate on a priority STEM population, with a composite effect size of 0.475 and several task-level gains. The intervention appears educationally meaningful, though evidence comes from a single institutional study rather than a broader multi-site trial.

interventions.use_case: computer-assisted formative feedback on a bank of mathematics test questions, with unlimited practice attempts before sitting class tests under exam conditions
online tutorial tasks used as practice resources with small grade credit, functioning as formative assessment support rather than full tutoring

finding.finding_summary: A quasi-experimental cohort comparison found better final-exam mathematics performance for the cohort with more formative assessment support. The composite score out of 20 was higher for Cohort 2 than Cohort 1 (means 10.88 vs 8.78; n=278 vs n=301), with effect size 0.475, indicating a meaningful improvement in learning outcomes on comparable exam tasks.
finding.measure: Scores on eight comparable final-exam mathematics tasks and a composite score out of 20, scored on a 0–5 SOLO-derived scale

finding.finding_summary: The added written assignment targeted clearer mathematical writing, complete explanations, and attention to evidence, and the study reports improved performance on tasks requiring structured reasoning. The findings suggest stronger relational understanding and better ability to present valid arguments, with several task-level effects in the moderate range and one very high effect on the Mean Value Theorem task (d=0.70).
finding.measure: SOLO-derived quality of written mathematical solutions on final-exam tasks, especially proof/argument structure
finding.effect_size: 0.70 on Task 7; composite d/g reported as 0.475
